items.title: OpenAI partners with Google Cloud to offer frontier models and Codex workflows through Google Cloud Marketplace [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI and Google Cloud have partnered to integrate OpenAI's frontier models and Codex agentic workflows into Google Cloud's Model Garden, enabling customers to access these models natively within Google Cloud's infrastructure. This integration supports complex AI workflows at scale while providing enterprises with data governance and access controls suitable for regulated industries. The models will be available for purchase through the Google Cloud Marketplace, allowing enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments to apply those credits. OpenAI models will also be accessible soon in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, offering customers flexibility in model choice. General availability is planned in the coming weeks, expanding enterprise options for deploying frontier AI models within Google Cloud environments.

items.title: Claude launches Claude Duet, a proactive AI agent that manages tasks and briefs users daily, available in Pro and Max plans in the US [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Claude Duet is a proactive AI assistant designed to handle tasks of varying sizes, keep working autonomously, and notify users only when their input is needed. It integrates with over 6,000 connectors and plugins, operates with built-in judgment to prioritize user needs, and maintains continuity by using the same memory and skills as the Claude app. The service runs on users' own cloud computers to ensure privacy and requires user approval for sensitive actions like sending messages or making payments.

items.title: OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research use thousands of AI agents to analyze brain cell data and identify new biological research leads in 32 minutes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research deployed thousands of AI agents powered by GPT-Rosalind to analyze experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells, uncovering new biological connections relevant to diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. The AI agents linked gene disruptions to cellular effects and scientific literature, producing a reasoning atlas that highlights potential mechanisms and research directions. The distributed AI approach dramatically reduced analysis time from months or years to minutes, reproducing known findings and discovering additional leads, including differences in disease-linked genes and a possible link between cholesterol regulation and neurodegeneration. The reasoning atlas is publicly available to help scientists explore these insights and prioritize further experiments.

items.title: OpenAI leads global coalition to coordinate response and patch critical PHP vulnerabilities discovered using GPT-5.6 Sol [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI coordinated with PHP maintainers, security researchers, and providers like Wiz and Cloudflare to address critical vulnerabilities found in PHP using AI models, emphasizing the urgency for organizations to apply fixes. The initiative, called Patch the Planet, involved validating flaws, developing patches, and preparing protections ahead of public disclosure to mitigate widespread risk. The response included collaboration with government cyber agencies and infrastructure providers to protect critical systems and support organizations with limited security resources through subsidized AI access. OpenAI also proposed a scalable framework for coordinated vulnerability disclosure in the AI era, aiming to improve global security efforts as AI uncovers more software flaws.

items.title: OpenAI updates Usage Policies and aligns safety standards with partners to ensure consistent safeguards across services offering GPT-6 Astra and other models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services providing access to its models, including GPT-6 Astra, and is updating its Usage Policies effective November 20, 2026, to clarify rules for safe AI development and sensitive uses. The company evaluates model risks before deployment, monitors for misuse, and requires partners to maintain safeguards consistent with OpenAI's standards, investigating violations and coordinating enforcement across platforms. OpenAI is also introducing SafetyIDs to help identify misuse more precisely while protecting user privacy, aiming to support responsible access and clear expectations for developers and businesses using its AI models.

items.title: Meta shifts AI liability to enterprise customers in new terms effective October 30, also expanding rights to use content linked to Meta accounts [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta will update its commercial terms on October 30 to make enterprise customers legally responsible for any mistakes made by its AI models, including actions by partners or contractors. The new terms also grant Meta broad rights to use content associated with Meta accounts, including web scraping for advertising and business product development. The changes have raised concerns among consultants and security experts about data ownership, web scraping practices, and the transfer of AI liability to customers. Meta clarified that its web crawling applies only to ads and business products and respects robots.txt preferences, though the contract language has yet to be updated. Critics warn that the AI liability shift places undue risk on customers despite Meta controlling the AI models involved.

items.title: AT&T partners with OpenAI to enhance in-house legal work by improving knowledge access and automating intake processes for faster, more informed legal judgment [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: AT&T is collaborating with OpenAI to advance its LegalEdge initiative, aiming to streamline how its in-house legal team accesses expertise and manages incoming requests. The partnership focuses on building a natural language intake system that classifies and prioritizes legal matters, connects them with relevant precedents, and provides context to lawyers to improve efficiency. This system is designed to reduce the time lawyers spend gathering information, allowing them to focus more on applying their judgment. AT&T emphasizes that final decision-making authority remains with its legal professionals, while the technology supports better-informed and scalable legal advice across the company.

items.title: Techdirt essay argues AI opposes the original hacker and punk ethos of resistance and social betterment
items.content_text: An essay on Techdirt reflects on the early internet era when hackers and programmers acted as outlaws and advocates building tools to resist centralized control and promote social good. It contrasts this with the current AI landscape, suggesting that AI represents a departure from those punk values and that the possibility for peaceful change has closed, implying future struggles may be unavoidable. The author, identifying as a former hippie, expresses regret but acknowledges a realist perspective that conflict may be necessary due to those obstructing progress toward a better world.

items.title: Researchers say AI's rapid dominance may be depleting diverse research fields needed for future breakthroughs, risking innovation exhaustion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent paper argues that the intense focus on artificial intelligence research is drawing talent and resources away from other scientific fields, potentially reducing the diversity of ideas necessary for major innovations. This concentration may lead to a decline in the creative capacity of AI research itself, as the ecosystem that fosters cross-disciplinary breakthroughs shrinks. The study highlights trends since 2017, including a migration of researchers into AI and a narrowing of attention that could hinder the emergence of novel concepts. It warns that this 'monoculture' effect might limit AI's long-term progress by starving it of fresh perspectives and serendipitous discoveries that typically arise from a broader scientific environment.

items.title: Blackstone's Jas Khaira says concerns over AI infrastructure debt are exaggerated amid rising interest rates and market jitters [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Blackstone is heavily investing in AI infrastructure through its Blackstone N1 group, led by Jas Khaira, who emphasizes the firm's unique approach to financing AI compute with flexible capital structures. Despite recent market concerns about the large debt burdens of AI-focused neocloud providers like CoreWeave and Firmus, Khaira argues that fears are overblown, citing strong customer contracts and the ongoing high demand for compute resources. Khaira explained that rising interest rates and credit spreads have increased borrowing costs even for major tech companies, contributing to market volatility and the cancellation of Firmus' IPO. However, Blackstone continues to support AI infrastructure buildout, viewing its $1.3 trillion in assets as critical to meeting the capital-intensive needs of the AI transition.

items.title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg agrees to remain in California for eight years under new stock deal amid potential billionaire tax ballot measure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]

The agreement, reached with Meta's board, links his ability to sell new nonvoting shares to his continued residence in California, aiming to keep him close to the company's AI development efforts. The decision followed concerns from a special Meta board committee about the impact of Zuckerberg's potential departure on the company's leadership and AI ambitions. The new stock arrangement allows Zuckerberg to sell portions of these shares over eight years if he remains in California, with provisions for exceptions if the company relocates its headquarters. Recent polling suggests the tax measure may not pass, but the agreement reflects Meta's efforts to maintain stability amid regulatory uncertainty.

items.title: Report: Texas data center expansion could triple soot and double smog pollutants by 2031, reversing decades of air quality improvements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A surge in new data centers in Texas, driven by demand for generative AI infrastructure, could significantly increase air pollution to levels not seen since the early 2000s, according to a report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). The report warns that if all planned data centers rely on the current electricity grid mix, emissions of fine particle pollution and smog-forming nitrogen oxides could more than double within five years, erasing years of air quality progress. Texas leads the US in data center capacity with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction power demand, and it is expected to have four times more proposed data center capacity powered onsite than any other state. The environmental impact depends heavily on whether developers use renewable energy or gas turbines to meet electricity needs; onsite gas engines could cause the highest pollution levels, while pairing grid power with onsite renewables could reduce nitrogen oxide emissions by up to tenfold. HARC CEO John Hall emphasized that these trends threaten to undo decades of emissions reductions achieved by transportation and state policies.

items.title: Researchers argue AI enables enclosure of the scientific information commons, transforming shared knowledge into private wealth and undermining social systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This article examines how artificial intelligence provides tools that could enclose the scientific literature, traditionally viewed as an information commons shared by all. Drawing parallels to the historical enclosure movement that privatized English agricultural lands, the authors argue that AI-driven enclosure threatens to convert communal scientific knowledge into private assets, disrupting the social frameworks that support open information sharing. The article provides a historical and economic primer on commons and enclosure, highlighting differences between physical commons and information commons. It warns that AI-enabled enclosure, while not identical to physical enclosure, shares key features such as privatization and social harm, potentially representing a fundamental challenge to the current scientific ecosystem and knowledge sharing practices.

items.title: New Kid on the Block [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
How Thoma Bravo Found a Discount in a Hot Cybersecurity Market [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Cybersecurity has been a dealmaking bright spot amid the broader software gloom, fueled by bets that AI adoption will boost demand for security products. But it's been hard for private equity firms to get in on the sizzling sector. Corporate buyers have been snapping up cybersecurity companies, competition that makes it harder for private equity firms to buy at prices that leave room for attractive returns when they eventually sell. Rising interest rates further limit what the firms can pay in debt-heavy buyouts. That makes Thoma Bravo-backed cybersecurity company Proofpoint's agreement last week to acquire data security company Varonis Systems in a $6.3 billion deal a notable example of how private equity can still find an opening in a hot market. And the tech-focused private equity giant is likely to do at least one more deal around this size in the coming year. The proposed acquisition values Varonis at around six times forward annual recurring revenue, according to a person close to the deal. That's a discount compared to similar public companies like cloud security and compliance company Qualys, which is trading at around 8 times forward annual recurring revenue. Cybersecurity acquisitions were already booming heading into this year, including Alphabet's $32 billion agreement to buy Wiz and Palo Alto Networks' roughly $25 billion deal for CyberArk, both announced in 2025. But interest in the sector has intensified amid much-hyped releases of powerful models like Anthropic's Mythos and a series of hacking incidents and agents gone rogue. It could further increase after Wednesday's disclosure of AI finding a security flaw in open-source programming language PHP, which most websites use. "People ended up realizing that the...threat vector effectively multiplied to infinity," said Brian Thom, a managing director at middle market investment bank Brown Gibbons Lang & Co. with a focus on infrastructure software and cybersecurity. Cybersecurity mergers and acquisitions hit a record 170 transactions in Europe and North America during the third quarter, according to an Arrowpoint Advisory report from earlier this month. Corporate buyers have been particularly active, including Accenture, which this summer acquired a majority stake in industrial cybersecurity company Dragos, plus two smaller companies in deals with a combined enterprise value of more than $4 billion. Thoma Bravo, for its part, saw an opportunity as Varonis' stock price came under pressure. Varonis has spent recent years moving customers from licenses to cloud-based subscriptions, temporarily depressing revenue growth, and announced late last year it would phase out older software by the end of 2026. Its shares had tumbled nearly 50% from last October to around $33 this June, right before reports of a potential takeover surfaced. More broadly, some software-focused private equity firms are hunting for companies with depressed share prices but still-credible growth prospects that can hold up even under threat of AI disruption. And many are still nursing the hangover from a software binge during the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. The Varonis acquisition comes at a critical time for Thoma Bravo, which has owned Proofpoint since taking it over for $12.3 billion in 2021. Proofpoint is generating more than $1 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, excluding the proposed Varonis acquisition, the person said, while five years under Thoma Bravo ownership puts it at the point when private equity firms typically face growing pressure to cash out. Adding Varonis expands Proofpoint's capabilities beyond its traditional focus of protecting employees from cyberattacks, including phishing and other email threats, to securing sensitive corporate data and controlling who can access it, including employees and AI agents. Though Proofpoint has made previous acquisitions under Thoma Bravo, the Varonis deal is by far its largest and gives it a bigger foothold in AI-related defenses that could arguably help it become a more compelling candidate for an initial public offering. Thoma Bravo could be on the hunt for more multibillion-dollar cybersecurity acquisitions following the Varonis deal, which is set to close in the first half of 2027. "There's a finite number of very large cybercompanies that we can invest in," said Andrew Almeida, a Thoma Bravo partner who oversees cybersecurity and infrastructure software investments. The firm is particularly interested in companies that generate revenue from the growing use of AI agents rather than relying solely on traditional pricing models that charge based on the number of human users, he said, and it plans to have another deal similar to the size of Varonis within the next 12 months. "Having agentic revenue, not just an agentic vision, but agentic revenue, is a must. And then having a pricing model that can capture this upcoming and ongoing explosion of agents is also a must," Almeida added. Wobbly IPO Window All eyes are on when Anthropic will finally make its IPO paperwork public, marking one of the final steps toward its hotly anticipated debut. Anthropic announced it had confidentially filed in June, and by late summer was preparing for an IPO as soon as late September. Now the latest chatter is that the filing could appear by the end of this week. Other AI-related IPOs that initially looked poised to go ahead of Anthropic's have been pulled or delayed amid mounting concerns about the costs of financing data centers and chips, while the broader IPO market has lost momentum in the midst of Treasury volatility. That's raised questions about who will test the market next-and whether Anthropic's offering could revive IPOs in general. Some IPO advisers, however, say other companies may need to go public first, paving the way for the AI giant. "I don't think Anthropic going public is going to open the floodgates," said Edward Best, co-chair of Willkie Farr & Gallagher's capital markets practice. "I think that Anthropic is going to wait until the water starts moving, and then if Anthropic comes through, it's just going to widen the river. "They can't take the risk that they don't do well. They're going to wait until they see a better path, and then other people are going to join right afterwards," he added. items.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal. August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress. August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team. September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix. October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available. October 21, 2026: Public disclosure. Via Hacker News Tags: open-source, php, security, ai, ai-security-research

items.title: Hackers Used Claude and Grok to Automate Attacks on Banks [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: A hacking group called CyberCartel used a web of AI agents powered by models from companies including Anthropic, SpaceX and Chinese lab Moonshot AI to automate cyberattacks against more than 400 Latin American financial targets, according to an investigation by the cybersecurity startup Straiker. The research, shared exclusively with The Information, is one of the first detailed reports of cybercriminals using AI models to successfully automate attacks that break into financial institutions. The AI agents used by CyberCartel, which has long targeted Latin American businesses and whose latest targets included banks and payment apps, appear to have stolen passwords and customer data and to have accessed people's bank accounts autonomously with little human effort, the Straiker research shows.

items.title: OpenAI, Anthropic Should Cap Compute for R&D, Say AI Safety Advocates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Ideas are flowing fast and furious on how AI labs can "pace" AI development so safeguards keep up with the technology's smarts. Last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman laid out three scenarios he said have been considered in the industry, including merging all of the AI labs into a single entity to develop new AI safely or creating a global regulatory body like the International Atomic Energy Agency. In the background, a loose group of safety advocates and researchers have been pushing for AI companies to cap the amount of compute they put towards research and development, a limitation they argue would be particularly effective in slowing AI development. The researchers are proposing companies commit to dedicating at least some minimum share of their computational resources to safety or monitoring, and another minimum share to running AI for customers, otherwise known as inference. That would limit the share of compute that could be used to develop stronger AI capabilities through R&D, such as training new models.
